source_text:
High-entropy alloy (HEA) has garnered significant attention due to its innovative alloy design concept and remarkable mechanical properties as an advanced concept alloy. HEAs comprise 5 to 35 at% of five or more elements with comparable atomic radius and exhibit high configurational entropy, lattice distortion, and slow diffusion rate. Owing to these characteristics, HEA does not exhibit the formation of intermetallic compounds and tends to form single-phase solid solutions. Due to their distinctive composition and microstructure, HEA has exceptional mechanical properties.

Particularly, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEA), comprise refractory materials such as titanium, niobium, vanadium, molybdenum, chromium, tantalum, and tungsten and nickel-based HEA comprise FCC single-phase solid solutions exhibit outstanding mechanical characteristics at elevated temperatures. These properties are comparable to those of titanium and nickel-based alloys, which are extensively employed in extreme environments due to superior heat resistance and specific strength. However, most of the investigations primarily concentrate on the addition of titanium and nickel, thus precluding their usage as primary constituents in HEA. Consequently, no research has been conducted on HEA comprising titanium and nickel, which exhibit excellent properties.

queries.broad: For high-entropy alloys intended for extreme environments, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties? State the intervention without limiting its class, the proposed mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the temperature and application boundaries under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose outcome would falsify the hypothesis.
queries.problem_constrained: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.
queries.expert_context: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii, and are associated with high configurational entropy, lattice distortion, slow diffusion, and a tendency toward single-phase solid solutions rather than intermetallic compounds. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have shown elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving high-entropy alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition and a single-phase solid-solution starting state, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to its untreated baseline? Include the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting evidence from prior observations, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.
